blocks.text: “Thank your ladyship.” Mr. Guppy does so. “Now, your ladyship;” Mr. Guppy looks at a little slip of paper. He has written short notes on it about the points he plans to make. But whenever he looks at it, he seems to become completely lost. “I—O yes!—I put myself completely in your ladyship's hands. Your ladyship might complain about this visit to Kenge and Carboy, or to Mr. Tulkinghorn. If you did, I would be in a very unpleasant position. I admit that openly. So I am trusting to your ladyship's honor.”
My Lady is holding a screen in her hand. With that hand she makes a scornful movement. In this way she tells him that he is not worth a complaint from her.

“Thank your ladyship,” says Mr. Guppy, “that's quite satisfactory. Now—I—dash it!—The fact is, I wrote down a heading or two here. They show the order of the points I thought of mentioning. But I wrote them in a short form, and I can't quite work out what they mean. If your ladyship will excuse me, I'll take it to the window for half a moment. I—”

Mr. Guppy goes to the window and stumbles into a pair of love-birds. In his confusion he says to them, “I beg your pardon, I am sure.” This does not make his notes any easier to read. He grows warm and red. He holds the slip of paper close to his eyes, then a long way off. He murmurs, “C. S. What's C. S. for? O! ‘E. S!’ O, I know! Yes, to be sure!” Then he comes back. Now he understands.
“I don't know,” says Mr. Guppy. He is standing halfway between my Lady and his chair. “Has your ladyship ever happened to hear of a young lady called Miss Esther Summerson? Or to see her?”
My Lady looks straight at him. “I saw a young lady of that name not long ago. This past autumn.”
“Now, did your ladyship think that she looked like anybody?” asks Mr. Guppy. He crosses his arms and holds his head on one side. He scratches the corner of his mouth with his notes.
From now on, My Lady does not take her eyes off him.
I think your ladyship,” says Mr. Guppy, “can hardly remember Miss Summerson's face?”
“I remember the young lady very well. What has this to do with me?”

“Your ladyship, I do assure you of this. Miss Summerson's image is printed on my heart—I mention that in confidence. Some time ago I was on a short trip in the county of Lincolnshire with a friend. I had the honor of going round your ladyship's great house of Chesney Wold. There I saw your ladyship's own portrait. It was so like Miss Esther Summerson that it completely knocked me over. It knocked me over so much that, at that moment, I didn't even know what had done it. And now I have the honor of seeing your ladyship close up. (Since then, I have often been bold enough to look at your ladyship in your carriage in the park. I dare say you was not aware of me. But I never saw your ladyship so close.) And the likeness is really more surprising than I thought.”

Young man of the name of Guppy! In the past there were times when ladies lived in castles. They had servants close by who would do anything, right or wrong, if they were called. In those times, with those beautiful eyes looking at you as they look at this moment, your poor life would have been worth almost nothing. You could not have been sure of living even one more minute.
My Lady slowly uses her little hand-screen as a fan. She asks him again what he thinks his interest in likenesses has to do with her.

“Your ladyship,” replies Mr. Guppy, looking at his paper again, “I am coming to that. Dash these notes. O! ‘Mrs. Chadband.’ Yes.” Mr. Guppy pulls his chair a little forward and sits down again. My Lady leans back calmly in her chair. Perhaps she is a little less relaxed and graceful than usual. But her steady look never moves from him, not even for a moment. “A—stop a minute, though!” Mr. Guppy looks at his notes again. “E. S. twice? O yes! yes, I see my way now, right on.”
